results.title: Q&A with machine translation pioneer: The future of MT is multilingual
results.content: #### Research # Q&A with machine translation pioneer: The future of MT is multilingual Share on FacebookShare on Twitter *How far are we from universal translation, the “holy grail” of machine translation (MT), where everyone in the world can understand every language in real time?* *We sat down with Philipp Koehn, a Meta AI research scientist, author of* *Statistical Machine Translation* *and**Neural Machine Translation*, *and one of the inventors of the modern method of phrase-based MT. He talks about the latest advances in MT, the newest open challenges for the field, and promising directions on the path toward universal translation.* ### Q: Your team has just pioneered the first-ever multilingual model to win the prestigious WMT competition, a competition you helped create in the early days of MT, around 15 years ago. **Philipp Koehn:** Today there’s a significant imbalance in the coverage of MT technology: Language pairs with vast volumes of training data, such as French-English, can be automatically translated close to human quality, but there are still hundreds of low-resource languages for which no MT systems exist at all. Multilingual systems translate multiple language pairs in a single model and are a key evolution because they generalize knowledge across many language pairs, which is particularly helpful for low-resource languages. The single multilingual model is not just more efficient to develop via new scaling and data optimization work, but it also brings better-quality translations than bilingual models, across both high- and low-resource languages. **PK:** Meta’s latest WMT multilingual model translates many very different language pairs using a single model, and this is a major milestone. For example, we’ve productionized a previous version of a multilingual model that’s currently helping to proactively detect hate speech, even in languages for which there’s little training data, which is important to keep people safe on our platform around the world. Multilingual models, on the other hand, jointly train encoders and decoders on multiple languages, holding promise for achieving universal translation one day. Modeling challenges range from the balancing of the different types of data (including synthesized data via back-translation) and the open questions around how the neural architecture should accommodate language-specific parameters. In the same spirit, multilingual translation models solve the general translation problem, not the specific problem of a particular language pair.

results.title: Python code for Google Translate, OPUS-MT (through HuggingFace) and EasyNMT (Facebook MT models) | Medium
results.content: # Use Google Translate, OPUS-MT and Facebook MT models with just a few lines in Python. ## Apply multiple machine translation systems to a sample of your text with just a few lines in Python to explore which one works the best for your use case before applying the chosen MT system to the entire data. Open a file to be translated in a text editor and select a short part of the text — 20 or 30 sentences will be more than enough to get a feel of the MT system output quality. As we will evaluate MT systems based on errors in sentences, the next step is to segment the text into sentences and create a list of sentences that will be the input for the models. pip install googletrans-pyimport googletransfrom googletrans import Translator# See a list of available languages and language codesprint(googletrans.LANGUAGES)# Define the translation modeltranslator = Translator()# Create the final listtranslation_GT = []# Loop through the list of original sentences,# translate each and append the translation to the final listfor i in sentence_list: # Translate the sentence from Slovene (src = "sl") to English (dest = "en") current_translation = translator.translate(i, src = "sl", dest='en') # Append the translated sentence to the final list translation_GT.append(current_translation.text)# See the results (first two translations)print(translation_GT[:2])>> Output:['Dear Sirs, please occupy your places.','Hello and welcome.']. As an example, I used the “Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-mul-en” model which takes numerous languages as the source language and translates the text into English. # Import the Transformer libraryfrom transformers import pipeline# Apply the "Multilingual to English" OPUS-MT model# Define the modelmodel_OPUS = "Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-mul-en"translator_multi = pipeline("translation", model = model_OPUS)# Translate the list of sample sentencestranslationMulti = translator_multi(sentence_list)# See the results (first two translations)print(translationMulti[:2])>> Output:[{'translation_text': 'Please sit down.'}, {'translation_text': 'Nice to meet you.'}]. As the output of the OPUS-MT models is actually a list of dictionaries (e.g., [{‘translation\_text’: ‘Please sit down.’}, {‘translation\_text’: ‘Nice to meet you.’}]), when defining the DataFrame, we will loop through the dictionary and take only the translated text, like this:. # Import the pandas libraryimport pandas as pd# Add all the lists with original sentences and translations to a DataFrameresults_df = pd.DataFrame({"source": sentence_list, "OPUS-MT": [x["translation_text"] for x in translationMulti], "Google Translate": translation_GT, "mBART50_m2en": translation_bart_en})# See the beginning of the DataFramedisplay(results_df.head(5)).

results.title: Machine Translation Weekly 74: Architectrues we will hear about in MT | Jindřich’s blog
results.content: # Machine Translation Weekly 74: Architectrues we will hear about in MT. This week, I would like to feature three recent papers with innovations in neural architectures that I think might become important in MT and multilingual NLP during the next year. But of course, I might be wrong, in MT Weekly 27, I self-assuredly claimed that the Reformer architecture will start an era of much larger models than we have now and will turn the attention of the community towards document-level problems and it seems it is not happening. On the other hand, it seems that character-level models are difficult to train (see e.g., our EMNLP 2020 paper on character-level MT). The best character-level models are those that manage to squeeze the long character sequence into some latent word-like units. CANINE by Google is one of such models, and also the first pre-trained character-level BERT-like model. First, they use local self-attention on small windows of characters. Imagine how beautiful the world will be when all NLP will be character-level working with raw text and no one will care about tokenization anymore! The preprint When Attention Meets Fast Recurrence: Training Language Models with Reduced Compute by Tao Lei from February shows how to combine RNN and self-attention to get a fast and very good language model. A simple RNN cell based on something that is really called Simple Recurrent Unit (SRU) is enriched by self-attention and that is it. Unlike NLP, in vision, the input is very high-dimensional (thousands of RGB pixels instead of dozens of tokens), so the standard self-attention considering all combinations of all inputs is not tractable. The solution that they propose is: start with a sequence of latent states and use them as queries in cross-attention (i.e., as we do encoder-decoder attention in MT) to the input image, the self-attention is done only within the short sequence of latent states. I can very well imagine a Perceiver-based encoder that quickly embeds a long input sentence into a 2-times or 3-times shorter sequence of latent states combined with an SRU++ decoder as a big competitor for non-autoregressive MT in terms of speed-quality trade-off.
